title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 35 (Civil liability for mis-statements in prospectus)

content.overview: Section 35(1) provides that where a person has subscribed for securities of a company acting on any statement included, or the inclusion or omission of any matter, in the prospectus which is misleading and has sustained any loss or damage as a consequence, the company and every person who (a) is a director at the time of issue, (b) has authorised himself to be named and is named as a director or has agreed to become such director, (c) is a promoter, (d) has authorised the issue of the prospectus, and (e) is an expert referred to in section 26(5), shall (without prejudice to any punishment under section 36) be liable to pay compensation to every person who has sustained such loss or damage. Sub-section (2) provides statutory defences. Sub-section (3) imposes personal responsibility without limitation of liability where the prospectus was issued with intent to defraud or for any fraudulent purpose.
content.glance: Reliance on misleading prospectus statement/inclusion/omission + loss → compensation from company, directors, promoters, authorisers and experts; statutory defences; unlimited personal liability if fraud proved.
content.study:
Where a person has subscribed for securities acting on any statement included, or the inclusion or omission of any matter, in the prospectus which is misleading and has sustained loss or damage as a consequence, the company and every person who is a director at the time of issue, named as director or agreed to become director, a promoter, or who has authorised the issue of the prospectus, and every expert referred to in section 26(5), are liable to pay compensation (without prejudice to punishment under section 36). Statutory defences under sub-section (2) include withdrawal of consent before issue, issue without knowledge/consent with public notice, and (as regards expert statements) correct and fair representation with reasonable belief in competence and consent under section 26(5). Where it is proved that a prospectus was issued with intent to defraud applicants or any other person or for any fraudulent purpose, every person referred to in sub-section (1) is personally responsible without any limitation of liability for losses sustained by a subscriber on the basis of such prospectus.

Case-law framing (batch 2 — prospectus cluster)
• Ordinary s. 35(1) compensation is statute-driven. The claimant must prove subscription acting on a misleading prospectus matter and resulting loss; proof of common-law deceit is not required for ordinary compensation.
• Derry v Peek (1889) 14 App Cas 337 (HL) remains the foundational common-law authority on fraud in a prospectus representation: fraud requires knowledge of falsity, absence of belief in truth, or reckless carelessness as to truth. Honest belief defeats common-law deceit. That standard is especially relevant when s. 35(3) (intent to defraud / fraudulent purpose → unlimited personal liability) is in issue.
• Predecessor civil provision: Companies Act, 1956, s. 62.
• Primary-report line-level verification of Indian Supreme Court applications of s. 35 remains open. Not COMPLETE_LOCKED.

sections.heading: Cause of action
sections.body: Subscription for securities acting on any statement included, or the inclusion or omission of any matter, in the prospectus which is misleading, causing loss or damage.

sections.heading: Persons liable
sections.body: The company and every person who (a) is a director at the time of issue of the prospectus; (b) has authorised himself to be named and is named as a director, or has agreed to become such director; (c) is a promoter; (d) has authorised the issue of the prospectus; and (e) is an expert referred to in section 26(5).

sections.heading: Statutory defences
sections.body: No liability under sub-section (1) if the person proves: (a) withdrawal of consent before issue and issue without authority/consent; (b) issue without knowledge or consent and forthwith reasonable public notice on becoming aware; or (c) as regards expert statements, correct and fair representation and reasonable belief up to issue that the expert was competent and had given the consent required by section 26(5).

sections.heading: Fraudulent prospectus — unlimited liability
sections.body: Where the prospectus was issued with intent to defraud applicants or any other person or for any fraudulent purpose, every person referred to in sub-section (1) is personally responsible, without any limitation of liability, for losses sustained by a subscriber on the basis of such prospectus.

provisions.title: Civil liability for mis-statements in prospectus

examples.title: Investor loss on misleading prospectus
examples.body: An investor subscribes on the basis of a misleading profit forecast in the prospectus and suffers loss. Section 35 supports a compensation claim against the statutory classes of defendants, subject to defences.

examples.title: Director who withdrew consent
examples.body: A proposed director withdrew consent before issue and the prospectus was issued without that person’s authority. The defence under section 35(2)(a) may apply.

hypotheticals.question: Must the claimant prove fraud for ordinary section 35 compensation?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Ordinary section 35(1) liability is for loss from reliance on a misleading prospectus matter. Fraud under sub-section (3) escalates to unlimited personal liability.

hypotheticals.question: What does Derry v Peek add to a section 35 analysis?
hypotheticals.analysis: It supplies the common-law meaning of fraud (knowledge, absence of belief, or reckless carelessness). That is especially useful when s. 35(3) unlimited liability for fraudulent purpose is pleaded. Ordinary s. 35(1) compensation remains statute-driven and does not require proof of common-law deceit.

distinctions.title: Civil liability (s. 35) vs criminal liability (s. 34)
distinctions.left: Compensation for loss from reliance on a misleading prospectus matter
distinctions.right: Criminal liability of persons who authorise issue of a prospectus containing untrue or misleading statements (s. 447)

misconceptions.trap: Only the company can be sued for prospectus misstatements.
misconceptions.correction: Section 35 lists the company, directors, named/proposed directors, promoters, authorisers and experts under s. 26(5) as potentially liable.

misconceptions.trap: Fraud must be proved for any section 35 claim.
misconceptions.correction: Ordinary compensation under sub-section (1) does not require proof of fraud; sub-section (3) applies only where intent to defraud or fraudulent purpose is proved.

cases.name: Derry v Peek
cases.point: At common law, fraud (deceit) in a prospectus representation is proved only where a false statement is made knowingly, or without belief in its truth, or recklessly careless whether it be true or false. Honest belief in the truth of the statement is a defence to deceit.
cases.note: Foundational House of Lords authority. Especially relevant to s. 35(3) (fraudulent purpose / unlimited liability). Ordinary s. 35(1) compensation is statute-driven and does not require proof of common-law deceit. Not a decision under the Companies Act, 2013. Primary-report line-level verification of Indian applications remains open.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 35 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Prove subscription on a misleading prospectus matter and loss. II. Identify the defendant class under (1)(a)–(e). III. Test statutory defences under (2). IV. Address fraud/unlimited liability under (3) if alleged (Derry v Peek for common-law fraud meaning). V. Conclude.

examTips: Structure: reliance + loss + defendant class + defences.
Separate ordinary compensation from fraudulent unlimited liability.
Cite Derry v Peek for fraud meaning under s. 35(3); do not require it for ordinary s. 35(1).

relatedJudgments.name: Derry v Peek
relatedJudgments.point: Common-law deceit in prospectus: knowledge, absence of belief, or reckless carelessness; honest belief is a defence to deceit.
